Reference Points and Speed: Motion is a change in position relative to a reference point. Speed is the distance traveled divided by the time taken, v = d / t, with units such as m/s or km/h. Average speed uses the total distance and the total time. Instantaneous speed is the speed at one moment, like a speedometer reading. Rearranging gives d = vt and t = d / v. When a trip has several parts, add all the distances and all the times; never average the speeds.
Velocity: Velocity is speed in a given direction, so it is a vector. Average velocity equals displacement divided by time. An object moving at a constant speed but changing direction is changing its velocity. A round trip has zero average velocity because the displacement is zero, even though the average speed is not zero. Velocities can be compared in different reference frames: a passenger walking forward on a moving train has a velocity relative to the train and a different one relative to the ground.
Acceleration: Acceleration is the rate at which velocity changes: a = (v_final - v_initial) / t, measured in m/s^2. An object accelerates when it speeds up, slows down or changes direction. If acceleration points the same way as the velocity the object speeds up; if it points the opposite way the object slows down, which is shown by a negative sign when the velocity is positive. A constant acceleration changes the speed by the same amount every second. The final speed is v = v_initial + at.
Distance-Time and Speed-Time Graphs: On a distance-time graph the slope is the speed: a steeper line means a faster object, a horizontal line means rest and a curve that gets steeper means speeding up. On a speed-time graph the slope is the acceleration, a horizontal line means constant speed, and the area under the line is the distance traveled. For a triangle area use one half base times height; for a rectangle use base times height.
Free Fall and Gravity: A falling object with only gravity acting on it is in free fall. Near Earth's surface all objects accelerate downward at g = 9.8 m/s^2, no matter their mass, when air resistance is ignored. Starting from rest, the speed after t seconds is v = gt and the distance fallen is d = 1/2 g t^2. A feather falls slower than a coin only because of air resistance. When air resistance equals the weight, the speed stops increasing and is called terminal velocity. A thrown ball slows down going up, stops for an instant at the top and speeds up coming down, always with the same downward acceleration.
